propositions.text: The principal and associated Appellants, both Bahamian citizens, appeal the RPD's denial of their refugee claims.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX (the associated Appellant), both citizens of the Bahamas, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection.

propositions.text: The Appellants submitted new evidence in support of their appeals.
propositions.quote: They have submitted new evidence in support of their appeals.

propositions.text: The Appellants ask the RAD to set aside the RPD's decision and find them Convention refugees or refer back for redetermination.
propositions.quote: The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the determination of the RPD and either find them to be Convention refugees or refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Bahamian Appellants appeal the RPD's denial, submitted new evidence, and ask the RAD to set aside or refer back the decision.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA s.111(1)(a), the RAD confirms the RPD decision that Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection and dismisses the appeals.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. These appeals are dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeals under IRPA s.111(1)(a).

propositions.text: The Appellants alleged before the RPD they are a lesbian couple facing persecution due to sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The Appellants alleged before the RPD that they are a lesbian couple, and face persecution in their home country on account of their sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants alleged to the RPD they are a lesbian couple facing persecution for sexual orientation.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the claims on October 16, 2015, citing numerous inconsistencies and general lack of credibility in the Appellants' testimony.
propositions.quote: By a decision of October 16, 2015, the RPD rejected the claims. Citing numerous inconsistencies in their testimony, the panel found the Appellants were generally lacking in credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the claims due to inconsistencies and lack of credibility in testimony.

propositions.text: The Appellants argue the RPD erred by not making a clear finding on their sexual orientation and should have analyzed risk under IRPA s.97(1).
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit on appeal that the RPD erred by failing to make a clear finding with respect to their sexual orientation. Since the panel did not specifically find that they are not lesbian, they argue, the RPD should have undertaken an analysis of the risk they face upon return, pursuant to Section 97(1) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: They ask the RAD to accept numerous new pieces of evidence in support of their appeals.
propositions.quote: They also ask the RAD to accept numerous pieces of new evidence in support of their appeals.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue the RPD erred on sexual orientation findings and request RAD accept new evidence.

propositions.text: IRPA s.110(4) limits Appellants to evidence arising after rejection or not reasonably available or expected at rejection time.
propositions.quote: Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected1 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA s.110(4) limits evidence to that arising after rejection or not reasonably available or expected then.

propositions.text: Appellants must fully explain in their Memorandum how new evidence meets IRPA s.110(4) and relates to them.
propositions.quote: It is for the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of Section 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The court requires Appellants to fully explain how new evidence meets IRPA s.110(4) and relates to them.

propositions.text: IRPA s.110(4) sets a disjunctive test: evidence must arise after rejection, or be not reasonably available, or not reasonably expected to be presented before rejection.
propositions.quote: Section 110(4) establishes a disjunctive test. The RAD must first consider whether the proposed new evidence arose after the rejection of the refugee claim. If it did, the evidence meets the requirements of the section. If it did not, the RAD must consider whether the evidence was reasonably available for presentation to the RPD prior to the rejection of the claims. If it was not reasonably available at that time, it meets the requirements of Section 110(4). If the evidence did not arise after the rejection, and it was reasonably available, the RAD must consider whether the Appellants could reasonably have been expected, in their circumstances, to have presented the evidence to the RPD prior to the rejection of their claims. If they could not have been expected to do so, the evidence meets the requirements of the section.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains IRPA s.110(4) disjunctive test for new evidence admissibility.

propositions.text: If evidence arose before rejection, was reasonably available, and could reasonably have been expected to be presented, it fails IRPA s.110(4) and cannot be admitted.
propositions.quote: If the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the claims, was reasonably available, and could reasonably have been expected, in the circumstances, to be presented to the RPD prior to the rejection of the claims, the evidence does not meet the test in Section 110(4). The RAD does not have discretion to admit such evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states evidence available and expected before rejection fails IRPA s.110(4) and cannot be admitted.

propositions.text: Section 110(4) allows evidence not submitted to RPD because it did not exist, was unavailable, or could not reasonably be expected to be presented then.
propositions.quote: As the RAD understands it, Section 110(4) provides the Appellants with an opportunity to present evidence that could not have been submitted to the RPD - either because the evidence did not exist at the time of the RPD proceeding, or because it did exist but was unavailable, or because it did exist and was available, but the Appellants could not have been expected to present it to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.110(4) allows evidence not submitted to RPD due to nonexistence, unavailability, or reasonable expectation.

propositions.text: Newness of evidence depends on the event or circumstance it proves, not just the document's creation date.
propositions.quote: In considering whether the evidence arose after the rejection of the claims, the RAD will not restrict its analysis to the date on the proposed new evidence. In the RAD's view, a document's "newness" cannot be tested solely by the date of its creation; what is important is the event or circumstance sought to be proved by the evidence.

propositions.text: Old evidence remains old even if placed in a newly dated document, as with much of the Appellants' proposed evidence.
propositions.quote: Old evidence remains old evidence, even if it is placed in a new document with a recent date, as seems to be the case with much or all of the Appellants' proposed new evidence here.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds newness depends on the event proved, not document date; old evidence remains old despite new document dates.

propositions.text: Even if evidence meets s.110(4), RAD assesses credibility, relevance, and materiality before admitting it.
propositions.quote: Where a document meets the test in Section 110(4), as discussed above, the RAD will conduct a further assessment of that evidence. While Section 110(4) provides the RAD with factors to consider in assessing a document's "newness", these factors alone cannot determine the admissibility of new evidence in an appeal. To put it simply, if a document is lacking in credibility, or is irrelevant, or is immaterial to the issues to be considered by the RAD, it would make little sense to admit such document, even if it meets the test in Section 110(4).

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD further assesses credibility, relevance, and materiality even if evidence meets s.110(4).

propositions.text: RAD applies Federal Court of Appeal's Raza factors—credibility, relevance, newness, materiality—to new evidence, based on similarity to s.113(a).
propositions.quote: The RAD has, in many appeals to date, applied the factors set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in Raza. While Raza predates the introduction of Section 110(4) of the IRPA, it is based on the nearly identical wording of Section 113(a). The Court of Appeal held that new evidence should be considered for its credibility, relevance, newness, and materiality, in addition to any express statutory provisions.

propositions.text: Parliament likely intended Raza test to apply to s.110(4) given the near identical wording to s.113(a).
propositions.quote: The RAD presumes that Parliament, in creating Section 110(4), was well aware that this provision is almost identical in wording to Section 113(a) - which provides a strong indication that Parliament intended the test from Raza to be used by the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD applies Raza factors to new evidence, presuming Parliament intended this for s.110(4).

propositions.text: Federal Court accepted RAD's use of Raza factors in Iyamuremye and noted they are considerations, not determinative, in Ghannadi.
propositions.quote: In Iyamuremye, the Federal Court accepted the RAD's application of the factors in Raza to new evidence submitted on an appeal under the IRPA. Subsequently, in Ghannadi, the Court held that the RAD should consider the factors in Raza, but noted that these are merely considerations to be taken into account and not necessarily determinative of admissibility.

propositions.text: In Singh, the Court found Raza factors are not transferable to RAD appeals and strict application was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In Singh, the Court found that the factors in Raza are based specifically on the language of Section 113(a) and are not transferable in the context of an appeal before the RAD. The Court found that it was unreasonable for the RAD to strictly apply the Raza factors without distinguishing its own role from that of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) Officer who is bound by Section 113(a).

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes Federal Court rulings on Raza factors' application to RAD appeals, including Iyamuremye, Ghannadi, and Singh.

propositions.text: Singh held RAD must have flexible admissibility criteria to allow full fact-based appeals given strict timelines before RPD.
propositions.quote: In Singh, the Court wrote that: ...in order for there to be a "full fact-based appeal" before the RAD, the criteria for the admissibility of evidence must be sufficiently flexible to ensure it can occur. Often, the evidence at stake will be essential for proving the factual basis of the errors the claimant alleges were made by the RPD. This consideration becomes all the more pertinent in light of the strict timelines a claimant now faces for initially submitting evidence before the RPD.

propositions.text: Singh noted RAD should have leeway to allow claimant to respond to evidentiary deficiencies raised by RPD.
propositions.quote: When the RPD confronts a claimant on the weakness of his evidentiary record, the RAD should, in subsequent review of the decision, have some leeway in order to allow the claimant to respond to the deficiencies raised.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Singh that RAD must have flexible evidence admissibility to allow full appeals and respond to RPD evidentiary weaknesses.

propositions.text: Singh emphasized main issue is whether evidence was not reasonably available or could not reasonably have been expected to be presented.
propositions.quote: The Court also held that the "main issue is whether the evidence 'was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably (or normally according to the French version) have been expected in the circumstances to have presented.'"

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Singh emphasized the key issue is whether evidence was not reasonably available or expected to be presented.

propositions.text: Singh did not discuss Iyamuremye or Ghannadi but certified a question on Raza test's applicability to s.110(4).
propositions.quote: The Court did not discuss Iyamuremye or Ghannadi in its analysis of Sections 110(4) and 113(a). It did, however, certify the following question: * "In considering the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment officer and that of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board, sitting in appeal of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division, does the test set out in Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 for the interpretation of paragraph 113(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 apply to its subsection 110(4)?"

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Singh certified a question on whether Raza test applies to s.110(4), without discussing Iyamuremye or Ghannadi.

propositions.text: The question of Raza factors' applicability to s.110(4) remains unsettled with conflicting findings on reasonableness and error.
propositions.quote: The question of whether the Raza factors are applicable to evidence that passes the test in Section 110(4) is still unsettled. It has been found that the application of the Raza criteria by the RAD is reasonable; it has also been held that the application of those factors without modification is an error. The Raza factors have also been described by the Court as "useful guidance."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicability of Raza factors to s.110(4) evidence is unsettled with conflicting views.

propositions.text: RAD must consider new evidence beyond s.110(4) test, including IRPA ss.162(2) and 171(a.3), and not admit irrelevant or incredible evidence.
propositions.quote: While trusting that the matter will eventually be resolved by the Federal Court of Appeal, the RAD must nevertheless continue to consider new evidence, such as that which has been submitted in support of this appeal. Although it may be inappropriate to strictly apply the factors in Raza, given that they are not specific to Section 110(4) and were not crafted for use in an appellate process, the RAD's consideration of new evidence cannot end with the application of the test in Section 110(4). To limit its analysis to that provision would be to ignore other provisions of the IRPA - such as Sections 162(2) and 171(a.3). Such a restricted analysis would also require the RAD to accept "new" evidence even if it is irrelevant, immaterial, or lacking in credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD must consider new evidence beyond s.110(4), including other IRPA provisions, and exclude irrelevant or incredible evidence.

propositions.text: Denbel held courts must prioritize statutory text over policy or Hansard; Parliament intended same legal test for PRRA and RAD evidence admissibility.
propositions.quote: In Denbel, the Federal Court held that: [43] When interpreting legislative intent, the Court must give priority to the written text in the absence of any lexical ambiguity. The Court's opinions on best policy cannot supplant the text of the law; nor can select passages from the Hansard. In my view, Parliament intended these two provisions to enshrine the same legal test. If Parliament had intended to establish more flexible admissibility rules in RAD appeals, it would not have replicated the restrictive language which governs PRRAs.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Denbel that statutory text governs and Parliament intended same legal test for PRRA and RAD evidence admissibility.

propositions.text: The RAD will analyze proposed new evidence for timeliness, evidentiary value, and weight, beyond just Section 110(4) focus.
propositions.quote: The RAD will therefore undertake an analysis of any proposed new evidence, not only for its timeliness, which is largely the focus of Section 110(4), but also to consider whether it has evidentiary value and, if so, how much.

propositions.text: Factors in Raza are helpful guidance but the RAD would do a similar analysis even if disregarding Raza.
propositions.quote: While the factors in Raza are indeed helpful guidance, the RAD would undertake a very similar analysis even if it would completely disregard that decision.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will analyze new evidence for timeliness, evidentiary value, and weight, using Raza factors as guidance but not exclusively, says the court.

propositions.text: Section 171(a.3) IRPA allows RAD to base decisions on evidence considered credible or trustworthy in the circumstances.
propositions.quote: Section 171(a.3) of the IRPA allows the RAD to receive and base a decision on evidence that is adduced in the proceedings and considered "credible or trustworthy in the circumstances."

propositions.text: RAD must consider credibility or trustworthiness of proposed new evidence in addition to Section 110(4) factors.
propositions.quote: This provision makes it clear that, in addition to the factors in Section 110(4), the RAD must consider the credibility or trustworthiness of proposed new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Section 171(a.3) IRPA requires RAD to consider credibility or trustworthiness of new evidence beyond Section 110(4) factors.

propositions.text: Although IRPA does not mention relevance explicitly, RAD must assess evidence relevance.
propositions.quote: While the IRPA makes specific reference to the credibility of evidence received by the RAD, there is no corresponding provision which addresses relevance. However, in the RAD's view, it is obvious that evidence must be assessed for its relevance.

propositions.text: Case law supports assessing relevance of evidence.
propositions.quote: Apart from the support from the case law, it would be highly inefficient for the RAD to admit irrelevant evidence, and contrary to Section 162(2) of the IRPA, which requires all divisions of the IRB to "deal with all proceedings before it as informally and quickly as the circumstances and the considerations of fairness and natural justice permit."

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD must assess evidence relevance despite no IRPA provision, supported by case law and efficiency considerations.

propositions.text: RAD should consider relevance of new evidence even if it meets Section 110(4) test.
propositions.quote: It is therefore appropriate for the RAD to consider whether new evidence is relevant, even if it meets the test in Section 110(4).

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD must consider relevance of new evidence even if it passes Section 110(4) test.

propositions.text: RAD will consider whether new evidence is material, meaning it could have led to success if before RPD.
propositions.quote: The RAD will also consider whether the proposed new evidence is material. In Raza, the Federal Court of Appeal described this factor: "Is the evidence material, in the sense that the refugee claim probably would have succeeded if the evidence had been made available to the RPD? If not, the evidence need not be considered."

propositions.text: Raza's materiality standard may be too high for RAD appeals.
propositions.quote: This factor may, in the RAD's view, set an inappropriately high standard in the context of a RAD appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes RAD considers materiality of new evidence but finds Raza's standard too high for RAD appeals.

propositions.text: PRRA officers must not review RPD decisions but assess risk arising after RPD decision and before removal.
propositions.quote: An officer determining a PRRA application must not engage in a review of the applicant's negative RPD decision. The PRRA process exists to determine whether a risk to the applicant has arisen between the date of issue of the RPD's decision and the date of the applicant's pending removal from Canada,

propositions.text: PRRA usually occurs a year or more after RPD decision.
propositions.quote: A PRRA will in most cases take place a year or more after the RPD's decision.

propositions.text: Raza's materiality definition fits PRRA context: new evidence must be significant enough to change RPD outcome.
propositions.quote: In this context, the definition of materiality set out in Raza makes good sense: the new evidence must be so significant that it would have led to a different outcome before the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains PRRA officers cannot review RPD decisions and Raza's materiality fits PRRA context well.

propositions.text: RAD has broad powers to review RPD decisions for errors and substitute or refer back decisions.
propositions.quote: The RAD is not restricted to making a new assessment of the risk faced by the Appellant, though this could occur as a result of new evidence presented upon appeal. The RAD appeal is meant to be decided within four or five months of the RPD's decision. The Appellant may challenge the decision of the RPD, and the RAD has broad powers to review that decision for errors of fact or law, or mixed fact and law, to confirm the decision, to confirm on other grounds, to set aside the decision and substitute another, or to set aside the determination and refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

propositions.text: RAD may only consider admissible new evidence when deciding to hold a hearing under Section 110(6).
propositions.quote: It is of paramount importance that the RAD may look only to admissible new evidence when considering whether to hold a hearing under Section 110(6).

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD has broad powers to review RPD decisions and must consider only admissible new evidence for hearings under Section 110(6).

propositions.text: Raza's materiality definition is too restrictive for RAD appeals and may reject evidence showing RPD error.
propositions.quote: The Court's definition of materiality, which is appropriate for evidence presented in support of a PRRA application, seems overly restrictive when applied to evidence submitted in an appeal to the RAD. If the RAD were to apply the materiality factor as defined in Raza, it could lead to the rejection of evidence that is capable of showing that the RPD's decision was in error, only because that evidence is not so strong that it would have resulted in the acceptance of the refugee claim, had the evidence been before the RPD.

propositions.text: RAD assesses whether RPD decision was in error, not whether RPD decision would have been different.
propositions.quote: Further, the RAD is not asking - as the PRRA officer is under Raza - whether the RPD decision would have been different. The RAD is making its own assessment of whether the determination should have been different or whether the RPD decision was in error.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Raza's materiality too restrictive for RAD, which assesses RPD error rather than hypothetical different outcomes.

propositions.text: RPD often rejects claims for failure to establish identity and does not consider persecution evidence in such cases.
propositions.quote: For example, it is not uncommon for the RPD to reject a refugee claim on the basis that the claimant has not established his or her identity, and in such situations, the RPD is not required to go further to consider the evidence of persecution.

propositions.text: New identity documents presented on appeal might be rejected by RAD if Raza's materiality test applied.
propositions.quote: A claimant rejected by the RPD on the basis of identity - perhaps because identity documents were still in transit from the country of origin at the time of the refugee hearing - might appeal to the RAD and present as new evidence such recently received documents. However, those documents might be rejected by the RAD if it considers their materiality as defined in Raza: whether the refugee claim would probably have succeeded if the documents were made available to the RPD.

propositions.text: Establishing identity alone may not warrant acceptance of refugee claim, so new identity documents could be rejected as lacking materiality.
propositions.quote: In many cases, the establishment of identity in and of itself does not warrant the acceptance of a refugee claim, and therefore the Appellant's newly obtained identity documents could be rejected by the RAD as lacking materiality, even though they could be the basis for a successful appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RPD often rejects claims on identity grounds and Raza's materiality test might wrongly reject new identity evidence on appeal.

propositions.text: Raza's restrictive materiality approach conflicts with RAD's broad powers and focus on errors and protection status.
propositions.quote: In the RAD's view, this restrictive approach to materiality is not consistent with the broad powers given to the RAD. While the PRRA officer is required to focus on a single issue - risk to the applicant - the RAD is required to consider both whether the RPD decision is in error and, after having reviewed all of the evidence, whether the Appellant is a protected person.

propositions.text: RAD should focus on whether evidence affects outcome of RAD appeal, not RPD decision.
propositions.quote: An approach that focuses on whether the evidence is material enough to affect the outcome of the RAD appeal rather than the RPD's decision is therefore preferred.

paragraphs.summary: The court prefers RAD focus on whether evidence affects RAD appeal outcome, not RPD decision, rejecting Raza's restrictive materiality.

propositions.text: RAD will apply factors to new evidence passing Section 110(4): credibility, relevance, and materiality for disposition under section 111 IRPA.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the RAD will apply the following factors to evidence that passes the test in Section 110(4). (a) The RAD will consider whether the proposed new evidence is credible or trustworthy. (b) The RAD will assess the relevance of the evidence - whether it is capable, together with the other evidence in the record (including other admissible new evidence) of proving or disproving a fact at issue in either the refugee claim or the appeal. (c) The RAD will determine whether the evidence is material, in the sense that it could be capable of justifying, with or without the benefit of an oral hearing, as the case may be, a disposition under section 111 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD will consider credibility, relevance, and materiality of new evidence passing Section 110(4) for disposition under section 111 IRPA.

propositions.text: RAD may refuse to admit new evidence not meeting credibility, relevance, and materiality factors but may consider other factors too.
propositions.quote: If the proposed new evidence does not meet each of the factors above, the RAD may choose not to admit it. These factors, however, are not exhaustive, as the RAD may consider other factors as appropriate in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD may reject new evidence not meeting credibility, relevance, and materiality but may consider other factors.

propositions.text: Appellants seek to admit various letters and photographs as new evidence, dated mostly 2015.
propositions.quote: The Appellants ask the RAD to admit the following as new evidence. (a) A letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 2015, from XXXX XXXX, along with a copy of his photo identification; (b) A letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 2015, from XXXX XXXX; (c) A letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 2015, from XXXX XXXX, along with a copy of his photo identification; (d) A letter, XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2015, from XXXX XXXX, along with a copy of his photo identification; (e) A letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 2015, from XXXX XXXX XXXX, along with a copy of his photo identification; (f) A letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 2015, from XXXX XXXX, along with a copy of his passport identity page; (g) A undated and unsigned letter, purportedly from a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (h) A series of photographs, purportedly of the Appellants and others at community and social events in Canada; and (i) Another letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX named in document (g); this letter is signed, and dated XXXX XXXX, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants ask RAD to admit various letters and photographs as new evidence, mostly dated 2015.

propositions.text: Letters (a) to (e) are from friends and acquaintances, dated between XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, 2015.
propositions.quote: The letters in (a) through (e) are from friends and acquaintances of the Appellants. Each letter is dated in the time period between XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, 2015.

propositions.text: Appellants' refugee claims were rejected on October 16, 2015; letters appear to have arisen after rejection by date alone.
propositions.quote: The Appellants' refugee claims were rejected on October 16, 2015. This evidence, if judged only by the dates on the letters, appears to have arisen after the rejection of the Appellants' claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes letters (a) to (e) are from acquaintances dated around 2015, apparently after the claims were rejected.

propositions.text: Content of letters shows authors knew appellants for months or years, some since arrival in 2015.
propositions.quote: The author of document (a) writes that he has known the Appellants "for over 3 months now." The writer of document (b) says he has known the Appellants "personally as members of the LGBT community here in Canada and in the Bahamas...." The author of document (c) says he has known the Appellants since XXXX, 2015, when they arrived in Canada. According to document (d), the writer has known the Appellants for more than five years, in both the Bahamas and in Canada, and the author of document (e) has also known them for half a decade.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds letters' content shows authors knew appellants for months or years, some since 2015 arrival.

propositions.text: Old evidence with recent dates is not new evidence; letters' content is not new and did not arise after claim rejection.
propositions.quote: As discussed above, taking old evidence and placing a recent date on it does not create new evidence. There is nothing new about the content of these letters, and the RAD finds that they did not arise after the rejection of the Appellants' refugee claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds letters are old evidence with recent dates and did not arise after claim rejection.

propositions.text: Appellants should have presented this evidence earlier given sexual orientation was core claim and RPD noted deficiencies.
propositions.quote: Given that the core of the Appellants' refugee claims was their sexual orientation, they could reasonably have been expected to present this evidence to the RPD prior to the rejection of their claims. This is particularly true in the time period after their hearing, as the RPD pointed out to them the significant deficiencies with other letters they had presented.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellants should have presented this evidence earlier since sexual orientation was core and RPD noted deficiencies.

propositions.text: To meet Section 110(4), letters must not have been reasonably available before claim rejection.
propositions.quote: In order to meet the test in Section 110(4), then, these letters must not have been reasonably available to the Appellants prior to the rejection of their refugee claims.

propositions.text: Appellants say they received letters only after negative decision and could not provide them to RPD.
propositions.quote: In an affidavit accompanying their appeals, the principal Appellant writes, with respect to each document, that "I received this letter only after the rendering of the negative decision in my refugee claim, and as such, I was unable to provide this document to the RPD prior to the decision being rendered." The Appellants make a similar argument in their Memorandum: that the documents were not reasonably available to them because they were only provided after the rejection of their claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court states letters must not have been reasonably available before claim rejection; appellants argue they received letters only after negative decision.

propositions.text: Not seeking letters before rejection does not mean they were unavailable; letters show authors knew appellants for months or years.
propositions.quote: With the greatest of respect to the Appellants, the fact that they did not seek these letters until after the rejection of their refugee claims does not mean the letters were unavailable. In fact, the Appellants point to nothing in the letters which suggests they could not have been written in time for the RPD hearing; most of the authors make it clear that they have known the Appellants, and known of their sexual orientation, for months or even years.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds not seeking letters earlier does not prove unavailability; letters indicate authors knew appellants for months or years.

propositions.text: Letters (a) to (e) do not meet Section 110(4) test; evidence did not arise after rejection and was reasonably available.
propositions.quote: The documents in (a) through (e) do not meet the test in Section 110(4). The evidence in those documents did not arise after the rejection of the refugee claims, the Appellants could reasonably have been expected to present it to the RPD, and they have not established that it was not reasonably available to them.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes letters (a) to (e) fail Section 110(4) test as evidence did not arise after rejection and was reasonably available.

propositions.text: RAD would decline to admit or give little weight to documents even if they met Section 110(4) requirements
propositions.quote: Even if the documents did meet the requirements of Section 110(4), the RAD would decline to admit them, or would give them little weight.

propositions.text: RPD found numerous corroborating letters suspiciously similar and Appellants inconsistent in testimony
propositions.quote: the RPD considered numerous corroborating letters, and found them suspiciously similar. It also found that the Appellants provided inconsistency testimony with respect to the letters.

propositions.text: RPD concluded letters were fraudulently produced by Claimants to bolster claims
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the letters were "fraudulently produced by the Claimants in order to bolster their claims."

propositions.text: Appellants have not challenged RPD's finding of fraudulent letters on appeal
propositions.quote: The Appellants have not challenged this finding on appeal.

propositions.text: RAD reluctant to give weight to further letters presented on appeal due to prior fraudulent letters finding
propositions.quote: As the Appellants have been found to have created numerous false letters in support of their refugee claims, the RAD would be reluctant to give any weight to the numerous further letters they have presented on appeal, even if those letters met the statutory requirements for new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD would not admit or give weight to documents due to RPD's finding of fraudulent letters, unchallenged by Appellants.

propositions.text: Document (f) is a letter from landlord stating Appellants identified as lesbian couple when negotiating rental
propositions.quote: The document in (f) is a letter from XXXX XXXX, who states that he was the Appellants' landlord in the Bahamas. He writes that "when negotiating the rental agreement for my apartment they made it absolutely clear that they were a lesbian couple."

paragraphs.summary: The court states document (f) is a landlord's letter confirming Appellants identified as a lesbian couple during rental negotiations.

propositions.text: Letter's evidence did not arise after claim rejection though dated 2015
propositions.quote: Again, the evidence in this letter did not arise after the rejection of the Appellants' claims, even though the letter itself is dated XXXX XXXX, 2015.

propositions.text: Appellants provided RPD with an email from landlord lacking sexual orientation reference
propositions.quote: In fact, the Appellants provided the RPD with an email from XXXX XXXX XXXX, though this made no reference to their sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Appellants explain they requested detailed letter after hearing but received it only after negative RPD decision
propositions.quote: They explain to the RAD that "although I asked Mr. XXXX for detailed information about our rental agreement, the e-mail he sent lacked some of these details. Subsequent to the hearing, I requested a more detailed letter from Mr. XXXX, but he only provided this document to me after the negative decision was rendered by the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes letter's evidence did not arise post-rejection; Appellants say detailed letter was requested after hearing but received only after negative decision.

propositions.text: Appellants received initial email weeks before hearing but took no further action until after hearing
propositions.quote: The Appellants apparently received the initial email from their landlord on XXXX XXXX, 2015, some weeks in advance of their hearing. Although it said nothing about their sexual orientation, they did not appear to take any further action with respect to Mr. XXXX until after their refugee hearing.

propositions.text: No documentary evidence shows Appellants asked landlord for more detailed letter or when
propositions.quote: They have provided no documentary evidence to show that they asked XXXX XXXX XXXX for "a more detailed letter", or to indicate when they did so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellants received initial email before hearing but did not act further and provided no evidence of requesting detailed letter.

propositions.text: Document does not meet Section 110(4) test as contents did not arise after claim rejection
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that this document does not meet the test in Section 110(4). Its contents did not arise after the rejection of the claims.

propositions.text: Appellants could reasonably have provided document earlier as they submitted another from same author
propositions.quote: The Appellants could reasonably have been expected to provide this, as they submitted another document from the same author to the RPD, and claimed that he knew of their sexual orientation in the Bahamas and nevertheless rented to them.

propositions.text: Appellants have not shown document was not reasonably available before claim rejection
propositions.quote: They have not established that this document was not reasonably available to them prior to the rejection of their claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the document fails Section 110(4) as it did not arise post-rejection and was reasonably available earlier.

propositions.text: Even if document met Section 110(4), RAD would not admit or would assign no weight due to credibility issues
propositions.quote: Even if this document met the requirements of Section 110(4), the RAD would not admit it, or would assign it no weight, for reasons of credibility.

propositions.text: Appellants found to have produced fraudulent documents and do not challenge that finding
propositions.quote: As discussed above, the Appellants have been found to have produced and presented fraudulent corroborating documents, and do not challenge that finding on appeal.

propositions.text: Letter has deficiencies: misspelled Appellant's name twice, hand-written error correction also erroneous
propositions.quote: there are deficiencies on the face of the letter. The associated Appellant's name is misspelled twice; there is one hand-written alteration of the letter, in an apparent attempt to correct the error, but the correction too appears to be in error.

propositions.text: Author's name misspelled under signature with suspicious hand-written alteration
propositions.quote: More alarmingly, Mr. XXXX appears to have misspelled his own name under his signature; this appears to have been typed as "XXXX", with a hand-written line carefully applied to the right side of the "XXXX" to make it appear as an "XXXX".

propositions.text: Letter refers to attached rental receipts which are not attached
propositions.quote: Finally, the letter also refers to attached rental receipts, which are not attached.

propositions.text: Letter lacks credibility due to misspellings and missing attachments, so would not be admitted or weighted
propositions.quote: Even if this letter met the requirements of Section 110(4), the RAD would find it to be lacking in credibility, as it misspells one Appellant's name, misspells the author's name, and does not include the additional documents to which it refers.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the letter lacks credibility due to misspellings, alterations, and missing attachments, so would not be admitted or weighted.

propositions.text: Document (g) is undated, unsigned letter from XXXX XXXX stating Appellants have XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2015
propositions.quote: The document in (g) is an undated, unsigned letter, purported from XXXX XXXX of XXXX XXXX XXXX, stating that the Appellants have XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2015.

propositions.text: Letter's date unknown so RAD cannot assess if it arose after claim rejection; content clearly did not
propositions.quote: As the letter is not dated, the RAD cannot assess whether it arose after the rejection of the Appellants' refugee claims. Its content clearly did not.

propositions.text: Even if meeting Section 110(4), RAD would not accept letter as new evidence due to lack of signature, date, credibility, and reliability
propositions.quote: Even if this document met the requirements of Section 110(4), however, the RAD would not accept it as new evidence. It is unsigned and undated and therefore lacking in credibility and reliability.

propositions.text: Letter is not material as it does little to corroborate key claim elements
propositions.quote: Further, it is not material; even if it could prove that the Appellants have XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, this does little to corroborate the key elements of their claims.

propositions.text: RAD has no reason to believe XXXX XXXX XXXX indicates romantic or sexual relationship rather than friendship or roommates
propositions.quote: The RAD has no reason to believe that a XXXX XXXX XXXX is indicative of a romantic or sexual relationship between the Appellants, instead of a relationship as friends or roommates with shared expenses.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds document (g) undated, unsigned, not credible, not material, and not indicative of a romantic relationship.

propositions.text: Document (i) is dated and signed but contents did not arise after claim rejection
propositions.quote: For the same reasons, the document in (i) is not admitted as new evidence. That letter is dated and signed, but its contents did not arise after the rejection of the Appellants' refugee claims.

propositions.text: Appellants say they did not provide letter to RPD as unaware XXXX XXXX XXXX was relevant to claim
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that they did not provide such a letter to the RPD because they were unaware that their XXXX XXXX XXXX was relevant to their refugee claim.

propositions.text: RAD finds document not relevant as it does little to establish sexual orientation
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that this document is not relevant - it does little or nothing to establish their sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Even if meeting Section 110(4), document would not be admissible as not relevant or material
propositions.quote: Even if this document met the test in Section 110(4), it would not be admissible here, as it is not relevant or material.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds document (i) dated but not post-rejection, not relevant or material, and inadmissible despite Appellants' explanation.

propositions.text: Documents (h) are numerous pictures of Appellants at events claimed to corroborate sexual orientation
propositions.quote: The documents in (h) are numerous pictures of the Appellants posing at various events, which they claim are corroborative of their sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Some pictures dated before claim rejection and not admissible under Section 110(4)
propositions.quote: Some of these pictures are dated prior to the rejection of the Appellants' refugee claims, and are not admissible under Section 110(4).

propositions.text: Appellants argue they did not have access to photos until after negative decision and possession only after decision
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that they "did not have access to these until after the negative decision," and that the photographs "were not in [their] possession until after the decision was rendered."

propositions.text: Appellants' explanation for late possession of photos is unsatisfactory
propositions.quote: This is not a satisfactory explanation. Why did the Appellants not have their own photographs, and how did they manage to obtain them only after their refugee claim was rejected?

propositions.text: Photos not admissible under Section 110(4)
propositions.quote: These documents are not admissible under Section 110(4).

propositions.text: Even if meeting test, photos not material as hugging or event attendance does not establish lesbian orientation
propositions.quote: Photographs of the Appellants hugging each other, or attending at events apparently related to sexual minorities, simply do not and cannot establish that they are lesbian, as such actions and attendance are not restricted to lesbians or sexual minorities.

propositions.text: Photos arising after claim rejection not admissible as not material and cannot affect outcome
propositions.quote: For this reason, even the photographs which apparently arose after the rejection of the refugee claims are not admissible here - they are simply not material and cannot affect the outcome of the Appellants' refugee claims or of these appeals.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds photos mostly pre-rejection and inadmissible; even post-rejection photos are not material or outcome-affecting.

propositions.text: Appellants' proposed new evidence is not admissible in these appeals
propositions.quote: For all of these reasons, the Appellants' proposed new evidence is not admissible in these appeals.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes all proposed new evidence is inadmissible in these appeals.

propositions.text: IRPA sets grounds and remedies for appeal but not standard of review for RAD
propositions.quote: While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes IRPA provides appeal grounds and remedies but not RAD's standard of review.

propositions.text: Appellants submit RAD should independently assess evidence and decide merits of refugee claims
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that the RAD should conduct its own independent assessment of the evidence and arrive at its own conclusion on the merits of their refugee claims.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue RAD should independently assess evidence and decide refugee claims' merits.

propositions.text: Panel previously considered legislation and jurisprudence on RAD's role and deference to RPD findings
propositions.quote: In another decision, this panel considered at some length the legislation and jurisprudence concerning the role of the RAD. It assessed the nature of a RAD appeal and addressed the scope and degree of deference to be shown to findings of the RPD.

propositions.text: Panel reached conclusions on RAD appeal approach applicable here
propositions.quote: The panel reached the following conclusions, which it finds to also be applicable here, about the approach to be taken in a RAD appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court recalls prior panel's conclusions on RAD's role and deference to RPD findings apply here.

propositions.text: RAD will assess all evidence including RPD record and admissible new evidence, considering law, fact, and mixed questions
propositions.quote: The RAD will take the following approach in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD. It will assess all of the evidence, both that in the RPD's record and any admissible new evidence. It will consider questions of law, fact, and mixed law and fact raised by the Appellant and, where applicable, the Respondent.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD assesses all evidence and considers law, fact, and mixed questions raised by parties.

propositions.text: In a true appeal with no admissible new evidence, RAD independently assesses RPD record to determine if RPD was wrong
propositions.quote: Where the proceeding is a true appeal - that is, where there is no admissible new evidence, as is the case here - the RAD will consider the decision of the RPD, the submissions in respect of that decision, and determine whether the RPD's determination is wrong. As a true appeal is founded on the record, the RAD must conduct an independent assessment of the evidence in that record in order to determine the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD independently assesses RPD record in true appeals without new evidence to decide if RPD was wrong.

propositions.text: In hybrid appeals with admissible new evidence showing RPD error, RAD considers RPD reasons with new evidence to determine if RPD was wrong
propositions.quote: Where an appeal includes admissible new evidence that speaks to an error in the RPD's decision, it is a hybrid appeal, where the RAD must consider the RPD's reasons in light of the new evidence, which may establish that the decision of the RPD is wrong.

paragraphs.summary: The court states in hybrid appeals RAD considers RPD reasons plus new evidence to decide if RPD was wrong.

propositions.text: In limited de novo appeals with admissible new evidence changing claim nature, RAD considers new evidence and RPD record but does not ignore RPD findings
propositions.quote: Where an appeal presents admissible new evidence which establishes a new, changed, or heightened risk, or otherwise changes the overall nature of the claim, this will result in a limited de novo appeal. In some such cases, the decision of the RPD may be less relevant in light of the new evidence - that is, the new evidence establishes a risk or degree of risk, or other potentially determinative matter not considered by the RPD. Unlike a true de novo proceeding, however, the RAD will not ignore the RPD's record or the findings of the lower tribunal, as these may remain relevant to the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains limited de novo appeals involve new evidence changing claim nature; RAD considers new evidence and RPD record together.

propositions.text: RAD defers to RPD findings made from advantageous position, usually credibility and fact findings, unless reasoning incomprehensible or unsupported
propositions.quote: The RAD will recognize and respect findings which the RPD was in an advantageous position to make, which will normally include credibility findings and other findings of fact. Where such deference is to be shown, the RAD will not intervene unless the RPD's reasoning process is not comprehensible or the outcome of that process is not based on and supported by the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD defers to RPD credibility and fact findings unless reasoning is incomprehensible or unsupported.

propositions.text: Where RPD's determination is based on findings warranting deference, RAD assesses if reasoning is comprehensible and supported by evidence
propositions.quote: Where the RPD's determination is entirely based on findings which warrant deference - such as an overall lack of credibility, based on oral testimony - the RAD will, having conducted its own assessment of the evidence, consider whether the RPD's reasoning process is comprehensible and whether the determination is based on and supported by the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD reviews RPD's reasoning comprehensibility and evidentiary support when findings warrant deference.

propositions.text: RAD shows no deference where RPD has no advantage, applies correctness standard, substitutes findings or refers back if needed
propositions.quote: On matters where the RPD has no advantage, the RAD will show no deference and will apply a standard of correctness, engaging in its own analysis of the evidence and reaching its own conclusion to determine if the RPD was wrong. Where the RAD finds that its conclusion does not agree with that of the RPD, the RAD will substitute its own finding and determination or, if it is unable to substitute, will refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD applies correctness standard without deference where RPD has no advantage, substituting or referring back findings.

propositions.text: RPD failed to make a clear finding on their sexual orientation, which was a key element of their profile
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit on appeal that the RPD failed to make a clear finding with respect to their sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Since the panel did not disbelieve their sexual orientation, it was required to consider their risk under Section 97(1) IRPA and erred by failing to do so
propositions.quote: As the panel did not disbelieve this key element of their profile, they argue, it was required to consider their risk under Section 97(1) of the IRPA, and erred by failing to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue the RPD failed to clearly find on their sexual orientation and erred by not considering risk under Section 97(1) IRPA.

propositions.text: The Appellants do not challenge the RPD's credibility findings
propositions.quote: the RAD must note that they do not otherwise challenge the RPD's credibility findings.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the Appellants do not challenge the RPD's credibility findings.

propositions.text: Federal Court described the RAD appeal as directed at RPD decision, based on record at RPD decision time, and concerned only with errors of law, fact or mixed law and fact
propositions.quote: In sum, the appeal before the RAD (i) is directed at the decision of the RPD, (ii) unless new evidence is accepted, is to be entertained on the basis of the record as it was constituted at the time of the RPD's decision, and (iii) is to be concerned solely with the errors of law, of fact or of mixed fact and law that, according to the appellant, the RPD made.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court described RAD appeal as directed at RPD decision, on record at RPD time, concerning errors of law, fact or mixed law and fact.

propositions.text: Section 3(3)(g) of RAD Rules requires full and detailed submissions on errors and their location
propositions.quote: Section 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules requires the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions regarding the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, and where those errors are located.

paragraphs.summary: RAD Rules require Appellants to make full detailed submissions on errors and their location.

propositions.text: Appellants have not challenged RPD's credibility findings which were determinative of refugee claims
propositions.quote: Here the Appellants have not challenged the RPD's many credibility findings; they simply argue that those findings did not apply to their sexual orientation.

propositions.text: No basis for RAD appellate intervention on credibility findings as no errors pointed out
propositions.quote: The Appellants have not pointed out any errors in the findings that were made, and there is no basis for the RAD's appellate intervention with respect to those findings.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants do not challenge RPD's credibility findings which were determinative; no basis for RAD intervention on those findings.

propositions.text: RPD erred by failing to explicitly find they are not lesbian women or not in a same-sex relationship
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that the RPD erred by failing to make an explicit finding that they are not lesbian women, or that they are not in a same-sex relationship together.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue RPD erred by not explicitly finding they are not lesbian or in a same-sex relationship.

propositions.text: It would have been better if RPD made a clear statement, but RPD's analysis obviously rejected all alleged facts of their story
propositions.quote: It would have been better had the RPD made such a clear statement, and it is puzzling that it failed to do so. However, it is obvious enough from the RPD's analysis that it rejected all of the alleged facts upon which their story is based.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD should have made clear statement but analysis obviously rejected all alleged facts of Appellants' story.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellants are Bahamian nationals but made no finding on sexual identity
propositions.quote: At the outset of its reasons, the RPD made a finding with respect to the Appellants' identity. It concluded that they are nationals of the Bahamas - but made no finding with respect to their sexual identity.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Appellants are Bahamian nationals but made no finding on sexual identity.

propositions.text: RPD found numerous credibility concerns related to sexual identity and found letters were fraudulent
propositions.quote: The RPD went on to describe and analyse numerous credibility concerns which were directly related to the issue of sexual identity... The RPD concluded that the letters were fraudulently produced by the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found many credibility concerns on sexual identity and concluded letters were fraudulent.

propositions.text: RPD found negative evidence about associated Appellant's former lesbian relationships and contradictory evidence about family knowledge of sexual orientation
propositions.quote: The RPD also considered evidence about the associated Appellant's former lesbian relationships, and made a negative finding... contradictory evidence about how her mother learned of her sexual orientation.

propositions.text: RPD found landlord's evidence not corroborative of sexual orientation or relationship nature
propositions.quote: It also found that evidence from the Appellants' landlord was not corroborative of their sexual orientation or the nature of their relationship.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found negative evidence on associated Appellant's lesbian relationships and landlord's evidence not corroborative.

propositions.text: RPD made a global finding that the Claimants are not credible and their allegations are false
propositions.quote: Having considered all of these things, the RPD found "that the Claimants are not credible... the Panel does not believe them... the Claimants' allegations are false."

paragraphs.summary: RPD made a global finding that Claimants are not credible and their allegations are false.

propositions.text: RPD's global credibility finding must be understood as rejecting Appellants' claim to be lesbian and in a lesbian relationship
propositions.quote: While it is true that the RPD did not make a specific finding with respect to the Appellants' sexual orientation, the RAD concludes that the RPD's global credibility finding must be understood as addressing this matter... the RPD did not accept the Appellants' claim to be lesbian and in a lesbian relationship.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes RPD's global credibility finding rejects Appellants' claim to be lesbian and in a lesbian relationship.

propositions.text: RAD disagrees that RPD should have considered Section 97(1) risk as Appellants failed to establish credible evidence of sexual minority status
propositions.quote: The RAD disagrees. The Appellants failed to establish with credible or trustworthy evidence that they are sexual minorities... no residual evidence upon which to base a Section 97(1) analysis.

paragraphs.summary: RAD disagrees that RPD erred by not considering Section 97(1) risk due to lack of credible evidence of sexual minority status.

propositions.text: Appellants request an oral hearing before the RAD
propositions.quote: The Appellants request that the RAD hold an oral hearing.

propositions.text: RAD refuses oral hearing request as no new evidence was admitted
propositions.quote: As the RAD has not admitted any of the Appellants' proposed new evidence, it has no choice but to refuse this request.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants request oral hearing; RAD refuses as no new evidence was admitted.

propositions.text: RAD confirms RPD decision that Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection and dismisses appeals
propositions.quote: Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. These appeals are dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: RAD confirms RPD decision denying refugee protection and dismisses appeals.
